block-race: Two machines disagree, and no authority can settle it. Yet everything downstream has to act on one history. Nakamoto's answer is not a judge. It is a race, and rewriting it gets exponentially more expensive the longer you wait.
Mining is a biased coin flip based on hashrate. Energy is the price of rewriting history, and the honest majority just outspends the liar.
Forget both chains. Only the gap matters, and the coin is rigged seventy to thirty. From three blocks behind, barely 8 in 100 attackers ever reach zero. Each confirmation halves what is left.
Satoshi models the attacker's block count as Poisson with mean lambda = z q over p, then sums gambler's-ruin tails.
Tripling the attacker from 10% to 30% inflates risk by ~544x. Adversary size dominates.
What this really buys is finality with no one in charge: the cost of a lie, denominated in energy and time.
gradient-pinball: Every trained model is the end of a journey down a landscape like this. Walk it and you have a model. Reproduce it and you have a proof.
Measure slope, step against it, repeat. Each step is the locally steepest move.
Step sizes dictate distance. If too large, the system overshoots and diverges.
Momentum acts as a memory of past gradients. Side-to-side bounces cancel, downhill drift compounds.
Momentum replaces the condition number with its square root. A 1000-step journey becomes just 30.
In high dimensions, most critical points are saddles. Momentum and noise help escape them.
bcml: Three problems a ledger suits. Data poisoned by someone who still collects the reward. Models that leak. Weights that remember nothing.
Record every transaction in the run, and tampering stops being invisible.
Raw data never leaves its owner. Only parameters, transactions and results reach the chain.
But a record proves what happened, not that it was any good. That needs a second mechanism.
Proof of Work agrees by burning electricity on a puzzle worth nothing once solved.
So aim it at the model. Proof of Learning makes the training run earn consensus; Proof of Deep Learning covers the model itself.
Proof of Training Quality asks more: not that work happened, but that it helped.
Now the electricity buys a model. And it opens one hard question: how do you prove the run was real?
Then incentives. One contract accepts the data, prices it, and updates the model.
You are paid for the loss you removed. Submit noise and the term turns negative.
Stake a deposit. It comes back if the data holds up, and is forfeited if it does not.
In simulation the honest and the dishonest separate cleanly, and accuracy holds.
Does it work? DeepChain was built: a Corda prototype trained on MNIST.
Accuracy rises with every party who joins. Throughput falls with every party who joins.
LearningChain shows the same trade: privacy noise buys privacy and costs accuracy.
So the survey ends on the seams: scale, energy, and consensus designed for learning rather than currency.
A review that only sells the idea is worth nothing. One of those seams, proving the training really happened, became my dissertation.
determinism: A Level D simulator is legally the aircraft. Airlines log real type-rating hours on it.
So the numbers are regulation, not goals. The ceiling: 150 milliseconds, input to response.
Every stage spends it. Image generation takes the largest bite.
Not a target. A gate. Miss it and the hours flown do not count.
Helicopters get 100 milliseconds. A hovering rotorcraft is unstable, and the pilot closes the loop faster.
Inside it, a fixed cadence. At 60 hertz each subsystem gets 16.67 milliseconds.
Mean frame time is 8.6 milliseconds, half the budget. But a deadline is never met on average.
Count the frames instead. Four hours is 864,000 of them.
One bad frame in a thousand, a 99.9% success rate, is 864 stutters a session.
And that assumes failures spread evenly. They cluster, so the real thing is worse.
A simulator is not one computer. It is a rack, all publishing into one frame.
The frame ends when the last host finishes. Latency composes as a maximum.
Reliability composes by multiplication. Nine hosts at three nines give 99.1% clean.
One straggler is enough. A single host at 19 milliseconds makes the frame late for everyone.
So the budget is allocated and enforced per host. A system average constrains nobody.
None of it is real unless it is instrumented while the session runs.
Trust the overrun counter. Step time is sampled, so a spike hides between polls.
One bus overruns, the rest stay clean, and the engineer knows before the qualification test does.
Determinism is not optimised in at the end. It is a budget, enforced every frame, and proven by the instrument you ship with it.
cyberevent: Incidents surface publicly before they surface officially. Someone tweets that the bank app is down.
The difficulty is the ratio. In an open Turkish stream, real events are a handful in a thousand.
That rarity is not an inconvenience to engineer around. It is the centre of the problem.
There is no labelled Turkish corpus, so the vocabulary must be learned from an incident you already know.
The nic.tr attack of December 2015 gives three corpora: the quiet year, the day, the fortnight after.
TF-IDF says which words separate an attack from ordinary Turkish. Each candidate then faces an A/B test.
Too many keywords and the queue floods with false positives.
Too few and the event is missed, or noticed days late.
So both become acceptance criteria: catch nic.tr on the day, stay under thirty percent false. It met both.
Then the language pushes back. Turkish stacks suffixes, so one stem becomes dozens of surface forms.
To a bag of words those are unrelated tokens. The evidence scatters.
This is the low-resource penalty, and a bigger classifier does not fix it. Stemming does, before the classifier.
Which is the under-reported part: here, preprocessing decides more than the model does.
And count the right thing. Not sentiment, but the entity that can be attacked.
Each entity is judged against its own history, because normal for one is an alarm for another.
On 14 December, nic.tr jumps from two or three mentions to twenty-eight. The anomaly is the signal.
The scoreboard, stated rather than rounded: 437 documents, 29 detections, 22 real. About 76%.
The seven misses are published too. A rare-event detector earns trust by naming what it gets wrong.
jira: I learned decentralized coordination on the Aegean: forty boats, no race director steering them...
...order emerging from local decisions and shared rules.
Software wants the same thing at global scale, with agents that never sleep and increasingly are not human.
Put one manager in the middle and their load is every agent at once. Capacity is fixed; the queue is not.
Take the manager out and publish a price. Each agent reads one number, however many of them there are.
So stop assigning the work and price it instead. Will this bug be fixed by Friday?
An automated market maker always quotes a price, so there is always someone to trade against.
And the slope of that curve is the crowd's probability that the work gets done.
If nobody is working on it, the price is cheap. Cheap is the signal to act.
A developer who knows they can fix it buys in quietly at ten cents.
Then they do the work. Effort moves a price they hold, so the payoff tracks the contribution.
The merge is asserted to an oracle with a bond. Unchallenged, it settles at one.
Nobody assigned that bounty. A price discovered it. Which leaves the question this lab keeps returning to: when no one is in charge, who verifies the claim?
Remove the last human. An agent reads the repository and writes the ticket itself.
The loop closes: propose, price, work, settle, with nobody in it.
But the same agents now create the work and are paid for it. A fabricated ticket runs the identical path.
So bond the proposal, bar self-settlement, and pay only for what real work leaves behind: a failing test that now passes.
Price discovers what to do. Verification decides what was done. That second half is the open problem.
model-heist: I built systems to stop data leaking. Prevention always fails eventually. So once your model is out in the world, can you still prove it was yours?
A single large watermark is obvious and hurts accuracy. Loud signals cannot hide in quiet spaces.
Spread the mark across weights. Each nudge hides in the noise. A matched filter correlates the secret pattern: signals add coherently, noise cancels out.
This forms a Z-test. Innocent models center at zero. Stolen models shift right. A threshold balances detection and false alarms.
Marks stay below the noise, preserving utility. Signal scales with breadth. You buy certainty with width, not loudness.
The thief is trapped by geometry. Without the secret pattern, blind scrubbing wrecks utility before erasing the mark.
oracles: An autonomous system is handed a verdict: 'that's crop damage,' 'that's a valid claim,' 'that's a threat.'
It didn't run the model. It can't see the weights.
In a world where AI agents consume each other's inferences, this is the trust question.
Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning (zkML) solves this using advanced cryptography.
An off-chain computer runs the heavy neural network. As data flows through, it generates a 'shadow' of the execution.
That shadow compresses into a short proof, cheap to check and impossible to forge. It certifies that this exact model produced this exact output.
The smart contract cannot run the model, but it can cheaply verify the proof. If it fits, the result is mathematically guaranteed.
Cryptography is expensive. The 'Optimistic' approach uses raw economic game theory.
A node asserts a result and locks a massive financial bond (stake) on the blockchain.
A challenge timer starts. If anyone can prove the node lied, the liar's stake is slashed and given to the challenger.
If the timer runs out with no challenges, the result solidifies as absolute truth. No expensive math required.
proof-of-learning: Proof-of-Learning promised to show you trained a model, not downloaded it. Attackers faked it within a year. My dissertation asks whether that proof can be made unfakeable.
A model is not born at the finish line. It walks there step by step. The path is the asset, not the endpoint.
The proof is a diary of the run: checkpoints, data, settings. Signed, so nobody can edit it later.
A checker never re-runs the whole thing. It re-does only the biggest steps, which is exactly where a faker taking shortcuts would get caught.
Proving costs one honest run. Faking means running the whole training backwards, and the number of paths that could fit explodes, so it's astronomically harder.
SecurePoL adds a second lock: a mark woven into the model. A faker can copy the curve, but not a mark they never trained in.
When models are cloned and stolen, what matters is not what a model knows, but whether it can prove how it learned. My work makes that proof unforgeable.
redundancy-reactor: A Level-D simulator is a legally certified twin of a real aircraft. Before sign-off, its flight computers must agree, so you run three, and let the majority rule.
Systems fail only when a majority of voters fail simultaneously. Independent voters make failure exponentially unlikely.
For rare, independent faults, simply adding voters pushes the failure probability off a cliff.
When faults correlate, the cliff vanishes. Redundancy no longer protects you; they all fail together.
A rocket had identical units. A variable overflowed. Both units failed identically seventy-two milliseconds apart, voting unanimously to crash.
You cannot vote out a shared mistake. Diverse designs drive correlation to zero, restoring safety gains.
wm-compare: To make Proof-of-Learning unspoofable, I had to hide a mark inside a model. Four ways exist, and each falls to a different attacker. The first writes a pattern straight into the weights.
2. To verify it, the owner extracts the weights and calculates a statistical Z-score.
3. As the Z-score shifts past the threshold, the probability of coincidence drops to zero. The theft is proven.
But there is a catch: you need full access to the stolen weights to run this test.
If the thief hides the model behind a commercial API, you cannot see the weights to run a Z-test.
Instead, Black-box watermarks train the network to memorize specific 'Trigger' images during training.
You query the API with the Trigger. Normal images work fine, but the Trigger forces a massive, hidden backdoor activation.
The network inexplicably outputs a secret cryptographic label, proving beyond doubt it is your stolen model.
For Large Language Models, watermarking happens continuously during text generation.
A pseudo-random hash splits the vocabulary into a 'Green List' and a 'Red List'. The probability distribution is subtly skewed to prefer Green words.
As the LLM generates a paragraph, a natural text is statistically expected to be ~50% Green.
A watermarked text, however, will slowly build up to ~75% Green. The statistical deviation becomes undeniable proof of origin.
Instead of modifying the main task, you branch off the latent layers to train a secret auxiliary classifier.
This auxiliary head outputs a secret signature using a hidden feature space, completely isolated from normal operations.
A thief might discover and prune this auxiliary head to evade the watermark check at inference time.
Every watermark can be attacked. The one that survives is not in the model. It is in the record of how the model was made.
